chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Muhammad from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammoon from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Asamm from Karram who said:

I swore between myself and my soul that I would never eat food during the day until the Qa'im of the Family of Muhammad rises. I entered upon Abu Abdillah and said to him: 'A man from your Shia has made it a vow upon himself not to eat food during the day until the Qa'im of the Family of Muhammad rises.' He said to me: 'Fast, O Karram, but do not fast on the two Eids, nor the three days of al-Tashreeq, nor when you are traveling. For when al-Husayn was killed, the heavens and the earth and those upon them and the angels clamored, saying: 'O our Lord, do You permit us to destroy the creation until we uproot them from the fresh face of the earth for what they made permissible of Your sanctity and killed Your chosen one?' Then Allah revealed to them: 'O My angels, O My heavens, and O My earth, be quiet!' Then He uncovered one of the veils, and behind it were Muhammad and twelve of his successors. He took the hand of one of them and said: 'O My angels, O My heavens, and O My earth, with this one I will avenge this one upon them.' He said it three times.
And it came in a narration other than that of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kulayni: 'With this one I will avenge them, even if after a while.'

key_terms.أيام التشريق: The days of al-Tashreeq (11th, 12th, and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)
key_terms.استحلوا حرمتك: They made permissible Your sanctity (disrespected Your rights)
key_terms.قائم: The Riser (al-Qa'im), referring to the Mahdi

ai.seo_question: What are the exceptions to the vow of fasting until the appearance of the Mahdi according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Nu'mani’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* illustrates the concept of *kaffarah* (expiation) for a personal vow, where Imam al-Sadiq (as) permits Karram to maintain his day-fast while observing standard exemptions for Eid and travel. The narrative expands into a cosmic eschatology, linking the martyrdom of Imam al-Husayn (as) to the eventual vindication of the Ahl al-Bayt through the twelve Imams, emphasizing that divine justice may be delayed but is inevitable.
